Accelerating Mathematical Discovery · Santa Cruz

alphaCentaur

Research mathematics with an AI collaborator: a worked example

Nic Brody · UC Santa Cruz

~0:00–0:30. This talk is a worked example. One research problem, a tool I built with an AI coding agent to attack it, and the workspace I built so that the human–AI collaboration stays honest. Then a live demo, and some advice for the working groups later this week.

The name

Centaurs, and Alpha-everything

  • Centaur is the chess word for a human–computer team. In the 2005 freestyle tournament, two amateurs with three ordinary PCs beat grandmasters with engines.
  • Alpha is DeepMind’s convention: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaFold, AlphaProof, AlphaGeometry, AlphaEvolve.
  • So: an Alpha-style system where the human stays in the loop.

weak human + machine + better process

beat strong human + machine + worse process.

And α Centauri is a binary star: A and B orbit a common centre. Neither one is the planet.

~0:30–2:00. The name is a mash-up. "Centaur" is the chess word for a human–computer team: in the 2005 freestyle tournament, where anyone could enter with any hardware, the winners were two amateurs running three ordinary computers, ahead of grandmasters who also had engines. Kasparov's reading of that was that the process mattered more than the strength of either the human or the machine. "Alpha" is DeepMind's naming convention — AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaFold, AlphaProof, AlphaGeometry, AlphaEvolve. So alphaCentaur is meant to be an Alpha-style system that keeps the human in the loop. And it happens that Alpha Centauri is a binary star, which is the app's icon: two stars orbiting a common centre.

This talk

A worked example in five parts

  1. A research problem: which groups of rational matrices are arithmetic?
  2. A tool built with an AI agent: the Presentation Calculator — and what went wrong.
  3. A workspace for the collaboration: alphaCentaur, and its rules.
  4. Live demo: the calculator running inside alphaCentaur.
  5. For your working groups: what has been AI-tractable for me, and a recipe.
~2:00–2:45. Here's the plan. The common thread is one research problem, so you see real mathematics rather than a toy.

I · A research problem

Which matrix groups are arithmetic?

Pick g1​,…,gk​∈PGL2​(Q) and let Γ=⟨g1​,…,gk​⟩. Its entries have finitely many primes S in their denominators, so

Γ≤PGL2​(Z[1/S])↪PGL2​(R)×p∈S∏​PGL2​(Qp​)acting onH2×p∈S∏​Tp​
  1. Is Γ Zariski dense?
  2. Is it discrete at some place — in PGL2​(R), or on some tree Tp​?
  3. Does it have finite index in PGL2​(Z[1/S]) (S-arithmetic), or infinite index (thin)?
  4. What is a presentation ⟨g1​,…,gk​∣r1​,r2​,…⟩?
~2:45–5:00. The problem. Take a few 2×2 rational matrices and the group they generate. Clearing denominators puts it inside PGL₂(ℤ[1/S]), which sits as a lattice in a product of real and p-adic groups, acting on the hyperbolic plane times a product of trees. Four questions, in increasing order of difficulty: is it Zariski dense; is it discrete somewhere; is it S-arithmetic — finite index — or thin; and what's a presentation. For a single group these can be very hard; the thin-versus-arithmetic question has no general algorithm.

I · A research problem

An easy one, and a hard one

Easy

Γ=⟨T,S,diag(2,1)⟩ with T=(10​11​), S=(01​−10​).

Zariski dense; not discrete at R or Q2​; index 2 in PGL2​(Z[21​]) by coset enumeration, in 3 ms.

Presentation: a graph of groups on the tree T3​, five relations.

Hard

Γ=⟨g=(01​1−2​),w=(03​20​)⟩ with S={2,3}

Not discrete at R, Q2​ or Q3​. Its congruence closure has index 960, but coset enumeration with 20 million cosets doesn’t close.

Of the elements of the closure of height ≤ 100, Γ reaches 157 of 5319. Probably thin (≅Z∗Z/2). No certificate.

~5:00–7:30. Two examples. On the left, translation, inversion and a diagonal matrix: the calculator decides in milliseconds that this has index 2 in PGL₂(ℤ[½]) and gives a presentation as a graph of groups on the 3-regular tree. On the right, two matrices, one an involution, with S = {2, 3}. It's non-discrete at every place, so no geometric argument works directly. The congruence closure — the smallest congruence subgroup containing it — has index 960, so if it were arithmetic its index would be 960. But coset enumeration with twenty million cosets doesn't close, and if you count elements of small height, the group reaches a vanishing fraction of its closure: 157 of 5319 at height 100. It looks thin, probably a free product ℤ ∗ ℤ/2. We have no certificate. (That density-by-height diagnostic was my idea; the AI ran it.)

I · A research problem

The Presentation Calculator

  1. Algebraic: Zariski closure, congruence closure.
  2. Geometric: each place — Poincaré’s theorem at R, Bass–Serre theory on the trees.
  3. Arithmetic: coset enumeration in a presentation of PGL2​(Z[1/S]), coverings, vertex orbits with Stallings folding, cusp certificates.
  4. Presentation: Poincaré, Reidemeister–Schreier, or a graph of groups.
~7:30–9:30. The tool. You type matrices — over ℚ or a number field — and press Compute. It runs four stages, in the browser, in parallel web workers: the Zariski and congruence closures; discreteness place by place, using Poincaré's polyhedron theorem at the real place and Bass–Serre theory on the trees; then the arithmetic stage, which tries several certificates of finite index; and finally a presentation. Every "yes" it prints comes with a certificate it checked exactly. Every "I don't know" is labelled as such.

  • Plus a batch pipeline that runs the page’s own code over thousands of groups.
~9:30–11:00. The calculator existed in a small form last year. The version you'll see was built over about two weeks this month, with a coding agent — Claude Code — that had a shell in my website's repository. It wrote most of the code: classical combinatorial group theory algorithms, each of which is a paper's worth of careful implementation, plus a batch pipeline that runs the same code over tens of thousands of groups. II · Building it with an AI agent

Who did what

The agent

  • Implemented algorithms from papers and specs, fast.
  • Ran thousands of examples, sorted the failures, profiled.
  • Cross-checked methods against each other, and against GAP.
  • Wrote exact research scripts for one-off questions.
  • Kept a running log — in a memory file it wrote for itself.

Me

  • Chose the questions, and the order to attack them.
  • Brought the structure: a finite-index subgroup of PGL2​(Z) forces S-arithmeticity (no covering needed).
  • Invented the density-by-height diagnostic.
  • Pushed back: “too specialized — check against Vaserstein and Benoist–Oh”; new methods must help typical groups, not just a test suite.
  • Decided what counted as a certificate.
~11:00–13:00. The division of labour. The agent is extraordinary at implementation and at sweeping: give it Todd–Coxeter and it writes Todd–Coxeter, then runs it on twenty thousand groups and tells you which ones time out. What it didn't do was decide what mattered. Several of the big wins came from me supplying a piece of structure — for instance a lemma from an appendix of a paper of mine: a group containing a finite-index subgroup of PGL₂(ℤ) is automatically S-arithmetic, so no covering argument is needed. And I had to keep pushing back on over-specialization: at one point it had built Bianchi-group machinery that only worked for three fields, and the right move was to go back to Vaserstein's theorem and Benoist–Oh, which work for every number field. [Nic: the arXiv reference for the appendix is 2308.07785; confirm the wording you want.]

II · Building it with an AI agent

Trust came from cross-checks

  • Congruence-closure index vs. coset enumeration: 400 S-arithmetic groups, 0 mismatches (313 exact, 85 lower bounds).
  • Vertex orbits vs. Todd–Coxeter on 246 groups: 221 agree, 0 disagree, 25 where Todd–Coxeter gives up.
  • Presentations vs. GAP: indices, abelian invariants and low-index subgroup counts agree.
  • Number fields vs. the theorems (Vaserstein, Benoist–Oh): 1,753 groups, 0 contradictions.

Two independent methods for every number I believe.

~13:00–15:00. Why should anyone believe a 13,000-line program written mostly by an AI? Not because the AI is trustworthy. Because every verdict can be reached two independent ways, and we compared them in bulk. The congruence closure is pure finite group theory; the coset enumeration is combinatorial; they agree on 400 groups. Vertex orbits on the product of trees agree with Todd–Coxeter on every group where both finish. Presentations were checked against GAP. Over number fields, the verdicts never contradict the known theorems.

II · Building it with an AI agent

What the cross-checks caught

Unsound certificate

A Bass–Serre test certified free products with edge inversions of order 2k > 2. Such an element fixes only an edge’s midpoint.

71 “discrete” records removed and rerun.

Wrong quotient

Level-by-level quotients PGL2​(Z/q) gave half the true index on ~3% of groups: the scalars of PGL2​(Z[1/S]) are only the S-units.

Caught by disagreeing with coset enumeration.

Wrong conclusion

“Coset enumeration doesn’t close, so it’s probably thin.” For rational Riley groups, a structural argument showed the index is finite and known: 2304 at 51/13.

Searching longer would never have found that.

~15:00–17:00. Three things that went wrong, all caught. One: a certificate that was simply unsound — the agent's Bass–Serre test accepted edge inversions of order more than 2, which fix only the midpoint of an edge. 71 database entries said "discrete" and shouldn't have. Two: a congruence computation that quietly assumed the wrong group of scalars and got half the index on about 3% of groups — found only because it disagreed with coset enumeration. Three, the most instructive: a wrong conclusion. On the rational Riley groups the machine kept failing to close coset enumerations, which nudged us towards "thin". The right observation was structural, and it turned every case into a finite-index problem with a known index. (That one is from this week's AIMing talk.) AI-written mathematical code is a conjecture generator until it's cross-checked.

II · Building it with an AI agent

Dead ends are results

  • Klein combination at ∞: 0 of 12 open groups.
  • Fricke’s trace test: sound, agrees with Poincaré on 334 groups — and decides none of the open ones.
  • Abelianization / congruence certificates of thinness: impossible in principle (thin groups are profinitely dense).
  • Ping-pong on boundaries of trees: led to a theorem.

Proved along the way

If Γ=A∗B is non-discrete at a place v and in the product of the other places, then no open ping-pong sets exist on ∏v​P1(Qv​) — for any free-product decomposition.

So no boundary ping-pong can certify the hard example.

~17:00–18:30. A lot of the work was failed attempts at a thinness certificate. We kept them all, with reasons. One failure became a theorem: for a free product that's non-discrete at one place and also in the product of the others, there are no open ping-pong sets on the boundary — so the classical approach provably can't certify our hard example. The agent is good at trying things; somebody has to write down why they failed, or it — or the next agent — will try them again.

~18:30–19:30. Where things stand. Over twenty-three thousand groups over ℚ, all small-height pairs up to symmetry: about 98% decided, each with a checked certificate. The open ones look thin, and the honest summary is that the bottleneck is now mathematical — we need a new kind of certificate — not computational. II · Building it with an AI agent

Where did the record of all this live?

  • The code: my website’s repository, mostly uncommitted.
  • The research log: a 140-line memory file the agent wrote for itself.
  • The results: 46,000 lines of JSON, rewritten as bugs were fixed.
  • Who wrote which lemma, which certificate, which conclusion: nowhere.

That is the problem alphaCentaur is for.

~19:30–20:30. Here's the uncomfortable part. The calculator was built in a coding agent with a shell on my disk. The research log for it is a memory file the agent wrote for itself. The results were rewritten every time a bug was fixed. And nothing records who contributed which idea or which line. For a tool that's fine. For research, it isn't: in three weeks I won't know which claims I checked. That's what alphaCentaur is for, and in the demo we'll move the calculator into it.

III · alphaCentaur

One workspace, one project per question

  • Runs on my Mac: a local web service and a native app. The iPad connects for handwriting.
  • A project owns its files, its chat and its runs. Nothing leaks between projects.
  • Bring your own model: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or a local Ollama.
~20:30–21:30. alphaCentaur is a local application: a small Node service with a SQLite database, a browser front end and a native Mac wrapper; the iPad pairs with it for handwritten notes. The unit is the project — one per research question — with its own files, its own conversation with the AI and its own computation history. It isn't tied to one AI company.

~21:30–22:15. Each project has these sections. Each is a reasonable version of a tool you already use; the point is that they share one store, one history and one AI collaborator.

III · alphaCentaur

A quick tour

Notes: live LaTeX

Computations: an AI-written exact check

Formalization: Lean

Manuscript: 140 pages, SyncTeX

~22:15–23:15. A quick tour, from my real projects: notes with live mathematics (the SO₃(ℚ) classification conjecture), a Python check the AI wrote for the Riley project, a Lean file, and a 140-page manuscript with source and PDF side by side.

III · The rules

Human and AI edit the same files.

Every editable artifact is shared — except one: description.md, which only the human may write.

No forks, no “AI copy” of the paper. A save names the revision it started from; a stale save fails instead of overwriting.

~23:15–24:15. Now the rules, which are the point. Rule one: human and AI edit the same files. The first version gave every file an owner — the AI could only edit its own files and had to copy mine. Since 15 September everything is shared, with one exception: the project description, which states the question, and which is mine. [Nic: say why you switched.] What makes sharing safe is bookkeeping: every save names the revision it started from, and if someone saved in between, it fails and your draft is kept.

III · The rules

Who wrote it, who may edit it, who checked it

Origin

Who wrote it

Human, AI, imported (authorship unverified), or mixed — recorded on every revision by the server, never by the model.

Permission

Who may edit it

Shared by default. description.md is human-only. Saved restrictions narrow what the AI may touch.

Review

Who checked it

Adopting, reviewing and checking are recorded separately. Editing a proof doesn’t make it correct.

Three separate records. Mixing them up is how “the AI proved it” sneaks into a paper.

~24:15–25:30. Three things that are easy to blur. Origin: who actually wrote this revision — recorded by the server; the model can't claim to be the human, and imported material I can't vouch for is labelled "authorship unverified". Permission: who may edit. Review: whether anyone checked it — a separate record. An AI editing a proof, or me adopting an AI proposal, says nothing about whether the proof is right.

III · The rules

What that looks like

An AI-written note says so: in its label, and in its first line.

Every change and every run, with who did it.

~25:30–26:15. A note the AI wrote in my Riley project: it carries the AI-created label, and its first lines say "AI-assisted working proofs for review… the main conjecture remains open; no priority claim is made." On the right, the activity log, human and AI entries interleaved.

III · The rules

Rules the model can’t talk its way out of

you › Never edit **/*.tex
you › Please never edit "my notes.md"
you › Do not modify notes/*.md

Plain sentences in the chat. Each becomes a saved rule before the model sees the message.

  • Saved in their own table, outside every file the AI can edit.
  • Included in every run, and checked again on every write — create, edit, rename, adopt.
  • Only a human can remove one.
  • Quoted documents and tool results can’t add or remove rules.
~26:15–27:15. Restrictions. If I type "never edit any .tex file", that sentence is parsed and saved as a rule before the message even reaches the model. It lives in its own table, and it's checked on every write. The model can't remove it, and text that merely passes through — a pasted paper, a web page, a tool result — can't create or delete one.

III · The rules

Evidence is append-only

CREATE TRIGGER revisions_no_update
  BEFORE UPDATE ON revisions
  BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'Immutable revision'); END;

CREATE TRIGGER revisions_no_delete
  BEFORE DELETE ON revisions
  BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'Immutable revision'); END;

The same two triggers guard the audit log and imported originals.

  • No revision or audit entry can be changed or deleted — not even by the app.
  • Imported originals are kept byte for byte.
  • A build or run records the exact revision of every input: later edits make it stale, never different.
~27:15–28:00. History can only grow. Revisions and the audit log are protected by database triggers, so not even a bug in my own code can rewrite them. A computation or a PDF build points at the exact revisions it used; if you edit afterwards, the result is marked stale, but never quietly changes.

III · The rules

What the AI can and can’t do

Can

  • read the files you select
  • create and edit files, as itself
  • propose a revision for review
  • run Python, LaTeX and Lean in a sandbox
  • look up references (Crossref)

Can’t

  • run a shell, or touch files outside the project
  • reach the network from a worker
  • see other projects, or your API keys
  • edit description.md or anything you’ve restricted
  • approve its own proposals

Every check is made by the server, on every call — not by asking the model nicely.

~28:00–29:00. The AI gets a small set of structured tools, not a shell. Contrast that with how the calculator was built: an agent with a shell on my whole disk. That's great for building software and not what I want for research records. None of this depends on the model behaving; the server enforces it on every call.

III · The rules

A report is a claim, not a certificate

  • The collaborator says: compiles, no axioms, no sorries, lake build successful.
  • The workspace makes that checkable without trusting the chat: the Lean file, its revisions, the check and its log are all in the project.
  • Whether we formalized the theorem we meant is still my job.
~29:00–30:00. A collaborator reporting a finished Lean proof. That report is a claim. What the workspace adds is that every piece of it can be checked without trusting the chat. And no tool can tell me whether the Lean statement is the theorem I actually care about. (This conversation is from the earlier version of alphaCentaur and was imported with the project.)

IV · Live demo

It runs in a sealed origin

  • Served from a second local port: its own origin, so it can’t touch the workspace or its API.
  • Web workers and ES modules work; the network stops at the project’s own files.
  • The URL carries a per-session capability for this project only.
~32:00–33:30 (backup). Running inside alphaCentaur. Until this week, project apps had to be a single HTML file. The calculator needs modules and eight web workers, so alphaCentaur now serves multi-file apps from a second local port — a separate origin, so the app can't script the workspace or call its API; its content-security policy keeps all traffic on the project's own files; and the URL carries a capability for this project only.

IV · Live demo

Two groups, two kinds of answer

PSL2​(Z): discrete at R, so Poincaré’s theorem gives ⟨g1​,g2​∣g22​,(g1​g2​)3⟩, index 2 in PGL2​(Z).

⟨T,S,diag(2,1)⟩: discrete nowhere, but index 2 in PGL2​(Z[21​]), matching its congruence closure.

~33:30–35:00 (backup). The modular group is discrete at the real place, so the presentation comes from Poincaré's polyhedron theorem. The other example is discrete nowhere, so geometry gives nothing directly; arithmetic does: coset enumeration finds index 2, and the congruence closure independently says 2 as well.

V · For your working groups

What has been AI-tractable for me

Good fits

  • Implementing known algorithms at research scale.
  • Sweeping thousands of examples and sorting the failures.
  • Cross-checking one method against another.
  • Exact scripts that verify one specific claim.
  • Literature lookups, conventions, boilerplate Lean.

Poor fits (so far)

  • Deciding which question matters.
  • Noticing the structure that makes a problem easy.
  • Certificates nobody knows how to state yet — like thinness.
  • Judging whether its own output is a proof.
~40:00–42:30. For the working groups on Saturday and Sunday: here is what has worked for me. The left column is where the agent multiplied what I could do by a large factor. The right column is where it was confidently wrong, or simply couldn't help. A good working-group problem lives on the left, and has a human on the right.

V · For your working groups

A recipe

  1. Write the question in a file only you edit.
  2. Ask for tools, not proofs: a calculator, a search, a checker.
  3. Two independent methods for every number you’ll believe.
  4. Keep the dead ends, with the reason each one failed.
  5. Label who wrote what, and keep the history.
  6. Put the rules where the model can’t edit them.
~42:30–44:00. A recipe, which is the talk compressed. You don't need alphaCentaur for any of it — a git repository and some discipline will do — but each step is something I learned by not doing it first.

V · For your working groups

Let the machine search.
Keep the judgement.

On the Riley groups the search kept saying “thin?”. The structure said “index 2304”.

~44:00–45:00. If you remember one thing: the machine is a superb searcher and a poor judge. The computer kept failing to close coset enumerations, which suggested "thin". A structural argument showed the index was finite and known.

One more thing

This talk was made in alphaCentaur

  • The Presentation section is a slide editor: live LaTeX, images, embeds, live applets, builds, notes.
  • A deck is one HTML file whose source is a JSON block inside it. The AI collaborator edits only that JSON.
  • The binary star is an applet: a few dozen lines of JavaScript, sandboxed.
~45:00–45:30. One more thing: these slides were made in alphaCentaur's own slide editor.

Next

What’s missing

  • A claims ledger: each claim with its status — conjectured, AI-argued, reviewed, Lean-checked, refuted — and what it depends on.
  • A “your turn” queue for the decisions only I can make.
